What role do teeth play at the beginning of the digestive process, and why does this step matter for the rest of digestion?
They break food into smaller pieces, creating more surface area so digestive juices can work more efficiently throughout the digestive system.
They produce saliva on their own, and that saliva is the only chemical step needed before nutrients pass directly into the bloodstream.
They pump digestive acid upward from the stomach into the mouth to chemically soften food before it is swallowed.
They generate heat that warms and softens food so the small intestine can absorb it without any further breakdown.

Teeth chew and grind food into small pieces. This mechanical breakdown increases the total surface area of the food, which allows digestive juices — including enzymes in saliva and stomach acid — to reach more of the food and break it down more efficiently. Without this first step, chemical digestion would be much slower and less complete.
Digestion begins in the mouth: teeth provide mechanical breakdown while saliva begins chemical digestion of starches.
Breaking food into smaller pieces increases surface area, making it easier for digestive enzymes in the stomach and small intestine to do their work.
